enonce_markdown: A small amount of phosphorus, which has five electrons in its outer shell, is added to pure silicon. What are the majority charge carriers in the semiconductor produced?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Doping a Group IV semiconductor with a Group V atom gives an n-type semiconductor; doping with a Group III atom gives a p-type semiconductor.

### Solution

Silicon forms four covalent bonds. A phosphorus atom uses four of its five outer electrons in bonds and the fifth is left **free to move**. The doped silicon is therefore **n-type** (n for negative) and its majority carriers are **free electrons**. Holes are the majority carriers in p-type material; protons and the positive ions of the lattice are fixed and do not carry the current.

**Answer: a.**

enonce_markdown:
(i) What is meant by rectification? *[1 mark]*

(ii) Name one electronic component used to rectify an alternating current and state the property that allows it to do so. *[2 marks]*
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A rectifier lets current pass in one direction only. It is used when an a.c. supply must be turned into d.c., for example in a phone charger.

### Solution

(i) **Rectification** is the conversion of alternating current (a.c.) into direct current (d.c.).

(ii) A **semiconductor diode** is used. It has a very low resistance when it is connected one way (forward biased) and a very high resistance when connected the other way (reverse biased), so it **conducts in one direction only** and blocks the other half of each a.c. cycle.

enonce_markdown: A 6 V battery, a lamp and a silicon diode are connected in series. The end of the diode marked with a bar (the cathode) is joined to the positive terminal of the battery. What happens to the lamp?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Conventional current flows through a diode from its anode to its cathode (in the direction of the arrow of its symbol). A diode connected the other way round is reverse biased and blocks the current.

### Solution

Here the cathode is joined to the **positive** terminal, so the positive end of the circuit is on the side where current would have to enter the diode against its arrow. The diode is **reverse biased**: its resistance is very high and practically no current flows, so the lamp stays off. A diode does not halve the current, and it does not heat up, because almost no current flows.

**Answer: d.**

choix.texte: The lamp lights at full brightness because current flows out of the positive terminal.
The lamp lights dimly because the diode halves the current.
The lamp lights for a short time and then goes out as the diode warms up.
The lamp stays off because the diode is reverse biased and has a very high resistance.

enonce_markdown: A single diode is connected in series with a resistor across a 50 Hz a.c. supply. Which description of the current in the resistor is correct?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A single diode gives half-wave rectification: it passes current only during the half-cycles in which it is forward biased and blocks the others.

### Solution

During one half of each cycle the diode is forward biased and current flows through the resistor. During the other half the diode is reverse biased and the current is practically zero. The current is therefore in **one direction only**, in **one pulse per cycle** (50 pulses each second). It is not steady d.c., because it falls to zero between pulses, and it never reverses, so it is not a.c.

**Answer: b.**

choix.texte: A steady direct current of constant value.
Pulses of current in one direction only, one pulse in every cycle of the supply.
An alternating current with a smaller peak value.
Pulses of current in both directions, two pulses in every cycle of the supply.

enonce_markdown: A pure silicon crystal is a poor conductor at a very low temperature, but its conductivity increases when it is warmed. Explain this behaviour, and say how it differs from what happens to the resistance of a metal wire when it is heated. *[3 marks]*
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The conductivity of a material depends on the number of free charge carriers. In a pure semiconductor, the carriers are produced by breaking covalent bonds.

### Solution

At very low temperatures, nearly all the outer electrons of silicon are held in covalent bonds, so there are almost no free charge carriers and the crystal is a poor conductor. When the temperature rises, more electrons gain enough energy to **break away from their bonds**. Each one becomes a free electron and leaves a hole, so the number of charge carriers grows and the **conductivity increases**. In a metal there is already a very large number of free electrons that does not change with temperature; heating makes the atoms vibrate more, which hinders the electrons, so the **resistance of a metal increases** when it is heated.

enonce_markdown: The 50 Hz a.c. mains supply is connected to a full-wave rectifier made of four diodes in a bridge arrangement, which feeds a resistor. How many pulses of current pass through the resistor each second?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A full-wave rectifier uses both half-cycles of the a.c., sending each one through the resistor in the same direction. A half-wave rectifier uses only one half-cycle in every cycle.

### Solution

An a.c. supply of frequency $f = 50\ \mathrm{Hz}$ has 50 complete cycles each second, and each cycle has two half-cycles, one positive and one negative.

Full-wave rectification turns every half-cycle into a pulse in the same direction, so the number of pulses per second is $2 \times 50 = 100$.

A single diode (half-wave) would give only 50 pulses per second. The count of diodes (four) does not multiply the number of pulses.

**Answer: c.**
